base_properties.human_readable: QWERTY Keyboard Layout as Natural Standard

stakeholders.name: keyboard_manufacturers
stakeholders.situation: Produce keyboards in a single dominant layout, achieving economies of scale and avoiding the inventory complexity of supporting multiple standards. The layout's universality means they face no competitive pressure to offer alternatives; any manufacturer could produce Dvorak or Colemak keyboards at comparable cost, but market demand is negligible because users are trained on QWERTY.

stakeholders.name: typing_instruction_industry
stakeholders.situation: Teach typing skills based on QWERTY layout. Curriculum, certification, and instructional materials are standardized around this layout. They could retrain on alternative layouts but face no market pressure to do so; the installed base of QWERTY users creates demand for QWERTY instruction, which perpetuates the installed base.

stakeholders.name: legacy_software_vendors
stakeholders.situation: Maintain software systems with keyboard shortcuts and interface conventions optimized for QWERTY key positions. Porting to layout-agnostic design would require non-trivial refactoring; the layout's stability means this cost is never incurred.

stakeholders.name: individual_typists
stakeholders.situation: Learn QWERTY because it is the only layout with widespread instructional support and device availability. Switching to an alternative layout after achieving QWERTY fluency requires unlearning motor patterns built over years; the cognitive cost is prohibitive for most. They bear the layout's inefficiencies (higher error rates, slower speeds for many letter combinations) as an invisible tax on their typing labor.

stakeholders.name: alternative_layout_advocates
stakeholders.situation: Promote ergonomically superior layouts like Dvorak or Colemak, citing evidence of reduced finger travel and improved typing speed. They are structurally excluded from the coordination equilibrium: even when they demonstrate measurable efficiency gains, the installed base of QWERTY-trained users and QWERTY-optimized systems makes adoption prohibitively costly for any individual or organization.

stakeholders.name: economic_historians
stakeholders.situation: Study QWERTY as a canonical case of path dependence and lock-in. They document the layout's origins (mechanical typewriter jam prevention), its persistence after the mechanical constraint disappeared, and the coordination failure that prevents transition to superior alternatives. Their analysis frames the question: is this a natural equilibrium or a constructed one that benefits identifiable parties?

six_questions.coordination_function: Provides a universal typing interface standard, enabling keyboard production at scale, interoperability across devices, and a single training target for typing instruction.
six_questions.transfer_function: Moves the cost of layout inefficiency (slower typing, higher error rates, ergonomic strain) from manufacturers and instructors to individual typists, who bear it as an invisible tax on their labor. Moves the benefit of avoiding transition costs from individuals to institutions with sunk investments in QWERTY-specific systems.
six_questions.absent_voices: Alternative layout advocates and ergonomics researchers who have demonstrated measurable efficiency gains from non-QWERTY layouts are structurally excluded from the coordination equilibrium; their evidence is acknowledged but treated as irrelevant because the switching cost is prohibitive.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: If QWERTY disappeared overnight and no layout held incumbent advantage, the market would reorganize around the most efficient available standard (likely Dvorak or Colemak based on ergonomic evidence), manufacturers would retool within months, and typing instruction would shift to the new standard within a generation. The current equilibrium persists because of the installed base, not because QWERTY is the natural choice in the absence of history.
six_questions.founding_problem: Early mechanical typewriters jammed when adjacent keys were struck in rapid succession; QWERTY separated common letter pairs to reduce jam frequency.
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: The mechanical jamming problem was solved by the shift to electronic keyboards in the 1970s-1980s, a fact attested by keyboard engineering history and uncontested by any party. Economic historians, ergonomics researchers, and alternative layout advocates all agree the founding problem is obsolete; only the installed base and switching costs explain persistence.

commentary.narrative_context: The QWERTY keyboard layout was designed in the 1870s to prevent mechanical typewriter jams by separating frequently-paired letters. The mechanical constraint disappeared with electronic keyboards by the 1980s, yet QWERTY persists universally despite ergonomic evidence favoring alternative layouts. This constraint story examines the naturalization claim: is QWERTY's persistence a natural coordination equilibrium, or does it benefit identifiable parties who avoid transition costs at the expense of individual typists? The claimed type is mountain (the layout is presented as a natural standard), while the metrics describe modest extraction and the structural presence of beneficiaries who gain from the status quo.
key_agents: keyboard_manufacturers: organized beneficiaries (mobile exit) — gain economies of scale from single-layout production
typing_instruction_industry: organized beneficiaries (mobile exit) — gain from standardized curriculum and materials
legacy_software_vendors: organized beneficiaries (mobile exit) — avoid refactoring costs
individual_typists: powerless payers (identity_locked exit) — bear layout inefficiencies as invisible tax
alternative_layout_advocates: powerless excluded (constrained exit) — structurally excluded despite evidence
economic_historians: analytical observers — study as canonical path dependence case
commentary.logic_rationale: Extractiveness is low-moderate (0.18) because the layout's inefficiency imposes a diffuse cost on all typists, but the cost is small per individual and invisible (typing is slower and more error-prone than it could be, but users have no comparison). Suppression is low (0.22) because no party actively enforces QWERTY; it persists through coordination failure and switching costs, not coercion. Theater ratio is low (0.15) because the layout genuinely coordinates typing; the extraction is in the foregone efficiency gains, not in performative maintenance. Accessibility collapse is moderate-high (0.72) because alternatives exist and are demonstrably superior, but the installed base makes them practically inaccessible to most users. Resistance is low-moderate (0.28) because alternative layout advocates exist and produce evidence, but they cannot overcome the coordination barrier.
commentary.directionality_logic: Manufacturers, instructors, and software vendors are beneficiaries: they gain from the layout's stability and universality, avoiding the costs of supporting multiple standards or retraining. They have mobile exit (could switch to alternative layouts at comparable cost) but face no market pressure to do so. Individual typists are the payers: they bear the layout's inefficiencies as an identity-locked cost (switching after achieving QWERTY fluency requires unlearning years of motor patterns). Alternative layout advocates are excluded: their evidence is acknowledged but structurally irrelevant because the coordination equilibrium cannot be broken by individual action.
commentary.perspectival_gap: From the beneficiary seats (manufacturers, instructors, software vendors), QWERTY is a natural coordination equilibrium that emerged from historical contingency and persists because it solves the coordination problem efficiently. From the payer seat (individual typists), the same structure operates as a locked-in inefficiency that extracts a diffuse tax on their labor. From the excluded seat (alternative layout advocates), it is a coordination failure maintained by institutional inertia. The engine computes these divergences from the structural data; the claimed type (mountain) reflects the dominant framing, not an adjudication.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The founding problem (mechanical jamming) is dead, yet the constraint persists. This is the mandatrophy signature: the arrangement outlived its original justification. The six-questions analysis establishes that the world would rearrange if QWERTY disappeared (manufacturers would retool, instruction would shift, software would adapt), which contradicts the mountain claim that the layout is a natural fact. The beneficiary structure is diffuse (no single party captures the gains), but identifiable parties avoid transition costs at the expense of individual typists. The receipt surface records this: gain_flow is diffuse (no concentrated capturer), fixing_cost is prohibitive (the coordination barrier is too high for any individual or small group to overcome).

omegas.question: Is QWERTY's persistence a natural coordination equilibrium that would re-emerge in the absence of history, or a constructed lock-in that benefits identifiable parties?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Natural experiment: if a jurisdiction mandated layout-agnostic keyboard design (all layouts equally available and supported) and neutral typing instruction (students learn the most efficient layout for their language), would QWERTY remain dominant or would alternatives gain market share?
omegas.impact: If QWERTY remains dominant under neutral conditions, it is a genuine coordination equilibrium (mountain). If alternatives gain substantial share, the current equilibrium is constructed and benefits parties who avoid transition costs (false summit, reclassify to tangled_rope).
omegas.description: Whether QWERTY is a natural equilibrium or a constructed lock-in.

omegas.question: Do the identified beneficiaries (manufacturers, instructors, software vendors) collectively capture enough value from QWERTY's persistence to constitute concentrated extraction, or is the benefit too diffuse to distinguish from general coordination surplus?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Economic analysis: quantify the cost savings manufacturers gain from single-layout production, the revenue instructors gain from standardized curriculum, and the refactoring costs software vendors avoid. Compare to the aggregate efficiency loss borne by typists.
omegas.impact: If beneficiary gains are concentrated and substantial relative to typist losses, the constraint is extractive (false summit). If gains are diffuse and comparable to coordination surplus, the constraint is closer to genuine mountain.
omegas.description: Whether beneficiary gains are concentrated enough to constitute extraction.

omegas.question: Is the switching cost (retraining all typists, retooling all systems) genuinely prohibitive relative to the efficiency gain from superior layouts, or is the cost overstated by parties who benefit from the status quo?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Cost-benefit analysis: measure the aggregate cost of transitioning to an optimal layout (retraining time, system refactoring, temporary productivity loss) against the aggregate benefit (faster typing, lower error rates, reduced ergonomic strain over remaining working lifetimes).
omegas.impact: If switching cost exceeds efficiency gain, QWERTY's persistence is economically rational (mountain). If efficiency gain exceeds switching cost, persistence is a coordination failure that benefits parties who avoid transition costs (false summit).
omegas.description: Whether the switching cost is prohibitive or overstated.

network.dual_formulation_note: This constraint is part of a potential kernel family examining path dependence and lock-in. The no-beneficiary reading would claim QWERTY is a pure coordination equilibrium (mountain with no beneficiaries); the beneficiary reading (this story) claims identifiable parties benefit from avoiding transition costs (false summit candidate). The two readings differ in their beneficiary structure and thus their ε values, warranting separate stories if the kernel is decomposed.
